When these popular car models debuted.Land Rover (Series I): Designed by Maurice Wilks on an Anglesey beach, it used aluminum bodies due to steel shortages and surplus RAF green paint.
When these popular car models debuted.Fiat Nuova 500: Dante Giacosa's tiny car, with a 479 cc engine, symbolized Italy's postwar economic boom.
When these popular car models debuted.Range Rover: The Louvre displayed it in 1990 as an exemplary work of industrial design, as it pioneered the luxury off-roader.
When these popular car models debuted.Honda Civic: Its CVCC engine meet strict US emissions rules without a catalytic converter.
When these popular car models debuted.Volkswagen Golf: Giorgetto Giugiaro designed it as the Beetle's replacement, and the GTI version helped create the hot hatch.
When these popular car models debuted.Honda Accord: Its name suggests harmony, and it was one of the best-selling cars in the US through the 1990s.
When these popular car models debuted.Toyota Camry: Its name comes from the Japanese word kanmuri, meaning crown.
When these popular car models debuted.Mazda MX-5 Miata: It revived the small, light roadster and holds the record as the best-selling two-seat sports car.
When these popular car models debuted.Toyota RAV4: The name stands for Recreational Active Vehicle with 4-wheel drive, and it helped popularize the compact SUV.
When these popular car models debuted.Smart Fortwo: Born of a Swatch and Mercedes partnership, it is only about 2.5 meters long and can park nose-in at the curb.

Olympic debuts of unexpected sports.Live pigeon shooting: At the 1900 Paris Games, it was the only time animals were deliberately killed in an Olympic event, and the event is never repeated.
Olympic debuts of unexpected sports.Plunge for distance: Divers glided without moving after plunging into a pool, and the winner was the one who travelled farthest, at the 1904 St. Louis Games.
Olympic debuts of unexpected sports.Art competitions: Medals went to architecture, literature, music, painting and sculpture until the competitions ended in 1948 over amateurism concerns.
Olympic debuts of unexpected sports.Solo synchronized swimming: This odd event ran from 1984 to 1992, beginning at the Los Angeles Games, and was held in a pool with only one swimmer.
Olympic debuts of unexpected sports.Beach volleyball: It debuted at the Atlanta Games in 1996, and the sport was then so unfamiliar there that the sand was trucked in.
Olympic debuts of unexpected sports.Snowboarding: At Nagano, Ross Rebagliati's gold was nearly revoked over marijuana, but he was allowed to keep it.
Olympic debuts of unexpected sports.Trampoline: The sport debuted at Sydney in 2000, where athletes bounce up to eight metres above the mat.
Olympic debuts of unexpected sports.BMX racing: The sport debuted at Beijing in 2008, using a dirt track with jumps and steep banked corners for fast races.
Olympic debuts of unexpected sports.Skateboarding: Tokyo's Games had teen medalists in this event, including 13-year-old Momiji Nishiya, one of the youngest ever to win Olympic gold.
Olympic debuts of unexpected sports.Breaking (breakdancing): Paris 2024 featured it, in the sport's formal name, but it was dropped from Los Angeles 2028.

Space agencies and companies by founding.NASA: Created in July 1958 after the Soviet Sputnik shock, it brought many earlier space and aviation programs under one roof.
Space agencies and companies by founding.CNES (France): France became the third nation to put its own satellite in orbit, Asterix, in 1965, a few years after this agency formed.
Space agencies and companies by founding.ISRO (India): Its Mars orbiter reached the planet in 2014 on the first attempt, on a budget less than the cost of a big Hollywood film.
Space agencies and companies by founding.ESA (Europe): Formed in 1975, with headquarters in Paris, it launches from Kourou in French Guiana, near the equator.
Space agencies and companies by founding.Roscosmos (Russia): It carries on the Soviet program and flies the Soyuz, which has ferried astronauts for decades.
Space agencies and companies by founding.Blue Origin: Founded by Jeff Bezos, its New Shepard suborbital rocket is named for Alan Shepard, the first American in space.
Space agencies and companies by founding.SpaceX: Elon Musk's company became the first private firm to dock a spacecraft with the ISS, in 2012.
Space agencies and companies by founding.JAXA (Japan): It formed from the merger of three agencies and its Hayabusa probes have returned samples from asteroids.
Space agencies and companies by founding.Rocket Lab: Based in New Zealand and founded by Peter Beck, its Electron rocket launches from the Mahia Peninsula.
Space agencies and companies by founding.UK Space Agency: Britain's own Black Arrow rocket orbited a satellite in 1971, then the program was cancelled.

How long these journeys take.Light from the Moon to Earth: Laser reflectors left by Apollo astronauts let scientists measure this distance, about 384,000 km, to within millimeters, and the Moon is drifting away by about 3.8 cm per year.
How long these journeys take.Light from the Sun to Earth: Sunlight's trip of about 150 million km means we see the Sun as it was over eight minutes ago, and a sudden vanishing would go unseen until then.
How long these journeys take.One orbit of the ISS: Astronauts on the station see about 16 sunrises and sunsets each day, and it travels at about 28,000 km/h.
How long these journeys take.Eurostar, London to Paris: The high-speed train takes about two hours twenty minutes through the Channel Tunnel, and this beats most flights once you count airport time.
How long these journeys take.Concorde, New York to London: Supersonic flights cruised at twice the speed of sound, and passengers could in effect arrive earlier than their departure time on the clock.
How long these journeys take.Apollo 11, Earth to Moon: The first crewed lunar landing mission took about three days to reach the Moon, and the craft's computer had less power than a modern pocket calculator.
How long these journeys take.Mayflower's Atlantic crossing: The Pilgrims' ship took 66 days to reach Cape Cod in 1620, and it was a cramped trip in which a baby was born at sea.
How long these journeys take.Phileas Fogg around the world: In Jules Verne's novel, this gentleman wins a wager by circling the globe in 80 days, helped by a day gained from crossing the date line.
How long these journeys take.Magellan expedition's voyage: Starting in 1519 with five ships and about 270 men, only one ship and about 18 men returned in 1522, and Magellan himself did not survive.
How long these journeys take.New Horizons, Earth to Pluto: The probe launched in 2006 flew by Pluto in 2015 at about 14 km/s, and gave humanity its first close-up images of the dwarf planet's icy heart.

When these law codes were issued.Code of Ur-Nammu: The Code of Ur-Nammu is the oldest known law code, from Sumer, and it used fines in silver rather than physical punishment.
When these law codes were issued.Code of Hammurabi: Hammurabi's Code is famous for 'an eye for an eye', and its laws are carved on a stone stele now in the Louvre.
When these law codes were issued.Draco's laws: Draco's laws in Athens were so harsh that the word 'draconian' came from them, with even minor crimes punished by death.
When these law codes were issued.Rome's Twelve Tables: The Twelve Tables were the first written Roman laws, displayed publicly in the Forum so everyone could know them.
When these law codes were issued.Theodosian Code: The Theodosian Code gathered Roman imperial laws since Constantine, and it was an important step in preserving them.
When these law codes were issued.Justinian's Code: Justinian's Code, the Corpus Juris Civilis, became the foundation of civil law in most of Europe.
When these law codes were issued.Taihō Code, Japan: The Taihō Code was Japan's first comprehensive legal code, which was based on Chinese law.
When these law codes were issued.Alfred the Great's laws: Alfred the Great's laws combined older Anglo-Saxon codes and the Ten Commandments, and set the foundation for English law.
When these law codes were issued.Magna Carta: Magna Carta was sealed by King John at Runnymede, and promised that even a king was subject to the law.
When these law codes were issued.Siete Partidas, Castile: The Siete Partidas, written under Alfonso X, was a legal code of seven parts, and it influenced the laws of Spain and the Americas.

Toy crazes, in the order they hit.Hula Hoop: Wham-O sold some 25 million within four months; the idea came from bamboo exercise rings that Australian children swung.
Toy crazes, in the order they hit.Lava lamp: Edward Craven Walker invented it after seeing a homemade egg timer of oil and wax bubbling in a pub.
Toy crazes, in the order they hit.Pet Rock: Ad man Gary Dahl sold ordinary stones in cardboard boxes with air holes and a training manual, and became a millionaire in months.
Toy crazes, in the order they hit.Tickle Me Elmo: Stores sold out and shoppers scuffled in the aisles in 1996 for the giggling, shaking doll from Tyco.
Toy crazes, in the order they hit.Bratz: Big-headed fashion dolls from MGA that challenged Barbie's dominance and set off a long legal fight with Mattel.
Toy crazes, in the order they hit.Webkinz: Each plush came with a code that unlocked a virtual pet world online, a hit with children from Canadian maker Ganz.
Toy crazes, in the order they hit.Zhu Zhu Pets: These robotic hamsters sold out in the 2009 holiday season at around ten dollars each.
Toy crazes, in the order they hit.Shopkins: Tiny collectible grocery figures from Moose Toys, an Australian company, were a pocket-money hit.
Toy crazes, in the order they hit.L.O.L. Surprise!: These dolls come wrapped in layers, so the toy's appeal was the unboxing, which exploded on YouTube.
Toy crazes, in the order they hit.Fidget spinner craze: Catherine Hettinger patented a spinning toy in the 1990s but let it lapse; it boomed in 2017 and many schools banned it.

When these disasters struck.Lisbon earthquake: It struck on All Saints' Day, followed by a tsunami and fires, and it shook the Enlightenment; Voltaire's Candide was a response.
When these disasters struck.Tambora eruption: This eruption caused 1816, 'the year without a summer', with crop failures across Europe and North America.
When these disasters struck.Krakatoa eruption: The explosion was heard thousands of kilometres away, and its tsunamis killed more than 36,000 people.
When these disasters struck.Johnstown Flood: A dam failure in Pennsylvania killed over 2,200 and drew Clara Barton's Red Cross into a major peacetime disaster response.
When these disasters struck.Halifax Explosion: A munitions ship collided with another in the harbour, causing the largest man-made explosion before the atomic bomb.
When these disasters struck.Tangshan earthquake: It struck at 3:42 am, and the official toll was around 242,000, making it one of the deadliest earthquakes in the 20th century.
When these disasters struck.Mount St. Helens erupts: The eruption shattered the top of the mountain, about 400 m, in the largest landslide in recorded history, and killed 57 people.
When these disasters struck.Bhopal gas leak: A pesticide plant owned by Union Carbide leaked a toxic gas, and it is regarded as the world's worst industrial disaster.
When these disasters struck.Chernobyl: The explosion happened during a safety test on reactor 4; the exclusion zone still stands but wildlife has thrived there.
When these disasters struck.Indian Ocean tsunami: A magnitude 9.1 quake off Sumatra on Boxing Day killed about 230,000 people across 14 countries and led to Indian Ocean warning systems.

When these tunnels opened.Thames Tunnel, London: The first tunnel under a navigable river, designed by Marc Brunel and finished by his son Isambard. It still carries London trains.
When these tunnels opened.Mont Cenis rail tunnel: It linked France and Italy under the Alps and pioneered the use of compressed-air drills in tunnel building.
When these tunnels opened.Gotthard rail tunnel: Hundreds of workers died digging it, and its chief engineer, Louis Favre, collapsed and died inside the tunnel in 1879.
When these tunnels opened.Simplon Tunnel: At roughly 20 kilometers, it was the longest railway tunnel in the world for decades, connecting Switzerland and Italy.
When these tunnels opened.Holland Tunnel, New York: The first mechanically ventilated underwater vehicle tunnel. Its chief engineer, Clifford Holland, died before it opened and it was named for him.
When these tunnels opened.Mont Blanc Tunnel: In 1999 a fire killed 39 people here and closed the tunnel for three years.
When these tunnels opened.Seikan Tunnel: This rail tunnel linking Honshu and Hokkaido was the world's longest until 2016 and runs about 240 meters below sea level at its deepest.
When these tunnels opened.Channel Tunnel: Crews dug from both countries, and when they met in 1990 their tunnels were within about half a meter of each other.
When these tunnels opened.Lærdal Tunnel: At about 24.5 kilometers it is the world's longest road tunnel; colored lighting caves break up the monotony for drivers.
When these tunnels opened.Gotthard Base Tunnel: About 57 kilometers long, it is the world's longest rail tunnel, bored beneath as much as 2,300 meters of rock.

When these European cities first appear.Paris (as Lutetia): Julius Caesar's account of the Gallic War mentions Lutetia, the island settlement of the Parisii tribe, which gave Paris its name.
When these European cities first appear.London (as Londinium): The Romans founded it after invading in AD 43; the first Londinium was burned down by Queen Boudica around AD 60.
When these European cities first appear.Dublin: Vikings built a fortified harbour here, and its name comes from the Irish Dubh Linn, the 'black pool'.
When these European cities first appear.Kraków: It was recorded by the traveller Ibrahim ibn Yaqub, and legend says it is named for Krakus, who defeated a dragon at Wawel.
When these European cities first appear.Copenhagen: The name means 'merchants' harbour', and in 1167 Bishop Absalon built the fortress that began the city's rise.
When these European cities first appear.Moscow: A chronicle records Prince Yuri Dolgoruky inviting an ally to a feast here in 1147, the date taken as its founding.
When these European cities first appear.Berlin: The date marks the first record of Cölln, the twin town across the Spree; Berlin appeared in 1244 and the two later merged.
When these European cities first appear.Stockholm: The name probably means 'log island', from stock and holm; the 1252 letter by Birger Jarl is its earliest known mention.
When these European cities first appear.Amsterdam: It began as a fishing village by a dam on the Amstel river, and in 1275 its people won toll exemptions from the Count of Holland.
When these European cities first appear.Warsaw: It became Poland's capital in 1596, when King Sigismund III moved the court from Kraków; WWII destroyed most of the city.

Finished TV shows by number of seasons.Firefly: Cancelled after only 14 episodes, aired out of order, yet fan campaigns won it a 2005 film sequel called Serenity.
Finished TV shows by number of seasons.Fawlty Towers: Just 12 episodes exist, written by John Cleese and Connie Booth, and Basil Fawlty was partly inspired by a real, rude hotel owner in Torquay.
Finished TV shows by number of seasons.Star Trek (original): NBC nearly cancelled it after season two, but a fan letter-writing campaign helped bring back this third and final year.
Finished TV shows by number of seasons.The Good Place: Created by Michael Schur, it is a comedy about the afterlife whose first-season finale twist rewrote everything that came before.
Finished TV shows by number of seasons.Breaking Bad: Creator Vince Gilligan pitched it as turning 'Mr. Chips into Scarface', following a chemistry teacher who becomes a drug boss.
Finished TV shows by number of seasons.Lost: Its pilot, about a plane crash on a mysterious island, was among the most expensive ever made at the time.
Finished TV shows by number of seasons.Mad Men: This 1960s advertising drama won the Emmy for best drama series four years running, from 2008 to 2011.
Finished TV shows by number of seasons.Game of Thrones: Based on George R. R. Martin's novels, it has won 59 Emmys, more than any other drama series.
Finished TV shows by number of seasons.Seinfeld: Famously 'a show about nothing', its 1998 finale drew about 76 million American viewers.
Finished TV shows by number of seasons.Friends: Its 2004 finale pulled in about 52 million US viewers, and its cast later reunited for a 2021 special.

The line ends with 'I don't give a damn', which was daring enough that the studio was fined for the word.
Famous movie lines, by the film's releas.Here's looking at you, kid: Rick says it as a farewell to Ilsa; it has since become shorthand for a tender goodbye.
Famous movie lines, by the film's releas.An offer he can't refuse: The American Film Institute ranked this among the greatest movie quotes ever, second only to the Gone with the Wind line.
Famous movie lines, by the film's releas.May the Force be with you: Obi-Wan's blessing is so well known that fans celebrate 'May the Fourth' as an unofficial Star Wars day.
Famous movie lines, by the film's releas.Phone home: E.T.'s raspy voice was largely performed by actress Pat Welsh, a heavy smoker at the time.
Famous movie lines, by the film's releas.I'll be back: Schwarzenegger reportedly struggled with 'I will' and the short contraction became his signature line.
Famous movie lines, by the film's releas.Show me the money!: Cuba Gooding Jr. won the Best Supporting Actor Oscar for his role in this film.
Famous movie lines, by the film's releas.I see dead people: A child actor, Haley Joel Osment, delivered it and was nominated for an Oscar for the role.
Famous movie lines, by the film's releas.Why so serious?: Heath Ledger's Joker says it, and he won a posthumous Oscar for the performance.
Famous movie lines, by the film's releas.Wakanda forever!: The film's crossed-arms salute became a cultural phenomenon, and it was the first superhero film nominated for Best Picture.

Clock speeds of famous processors.Intel 4004: It ran a desk calculator at 740 kHz, under a thousandth of the speed of a modern chip, yet started the microprocessor era.
Clock speeds of famous processors.Apple II: Steve Wozniak's design offered color graphics and built-in BASIC in a plastic case, and helped launch the home computer age.
Clock speeds of famous processors.IBM PC (1981): It used an Intel 8088, and the odd 4.77 MHz came from dividing the crystal frequency used in color television sets.
Clock speeds of famous processors.Original Macintosh: Its Motorola 68000 chip ran with just 128 KB of memory, and the machine famously introduced the mouse to the public.
Clock speeds of famous processors.Intel 386 at launch: As Intel's first 32-bit chip, it ran at modest clock speeds yet made modern multitasking operating systems practical on PCs.
Clock speeds of famous processors.Original Pentium: The original Pentium arrived in 1993 at 60 and 66 MHz, and its name came from the Greek word for five.
Clock speeds of famous processors.Cray-1 supercomputer: This 1976 supercomputer, shaped like a C with a bench built around its base, was the fastest in the world for years.
Clock speeds of famous processors.AMD Athlon (March 2000): AMD beat Intel to the 1 GHz milestone in March 2000, a race the two rivals had been waging for years.
Clock speeds of famous processors.Pentium 4 570J: Its NetBurst design pushed clock speed to the limit, and Intel then scrapped plans for 4 GHz after heat became a problem.
Clock speeds of famous processors.Intel Core i9-13900KS: It was the first desktop chip to reach 6 GHz out of the box, about 8,000 times the speed of the 4004.

Musical instruments, by when they were i.Piano: Bartolomeo Cristofori invented it in Italy as the soft-loud harpsichord, since it could play both quietly and loudly with the player's touch.
Musical instruments, by when they were i.Metronome: Dietrich Winkel invented it, and Johann Maelzel patented a version; Beethoven was an early fan who added tempo markings.
Musical instruments, by when they were i.Accordion: Cyrill Demian patented it in Vienna, and its free reeds vibrate as air passes through them.
Musical instruments, by when they were i.Tuba: Wilhelm Wieprecht and Johann Moritz patented it in Prussia, and it is the lowest-pitched of the brass instruments.
Musical instruments, by when they were i.Saxophone: Adolphe Sax patented it, and though it is made of brass, it counts as a woodwind because it uses a reed.
Musical instruments, by when they were i.Sousaphone: It is named for John Philip Sousa, who wanted a tuba that wraps around a marching player's body.
Musical instruments, by when they were i.Theremin: Soviet physicist Leon Theremin invented it, and it is played without touching, by moving hands near two antennas.
Musical instruments, by when they were i.Electric guitar: The Frying Pan, made by Rickenbacker, was the first commercially produced electric guitar.
Musical instruments, by when they were i.Hammond organ: Laurens Hammond made it as a cheaper alternative to the pipe organ, and it makes sound with spinning tonewheels.
Musical instruments, by when they were i.Moog synthesizer: Robert Moog's synth, popularized by Wendy Carlos's Switched-On Bach, brought electronic music into the mainstream.

When these famous car models debuted.Ford Model T: Ford's moving assembly line slashed building time dramatically, and over 15 million Model Ts were made by 1927.
When these famous car models debuted.Volkswagen Beetle: Ferdinand Porsche engineered it as a 'people's car' commissioned by Hitler's regime, and over 21 million were built.
When these famous car models debuted.Land Rover: Inspired by wartime Jeeps, early examples were reportedly painted in leftover military green because paint was scarce.
When these famous car models debuted.Mini: Alec Issigonis's design turned the engine sideways to give most of its footprint to passengers, and it won the Monte Carlo Rally in 1964.
When these famous car models debuted.Ford Mustang: It launched at the 1964 New York World's Fair, created the 'pony car' category and sold over a million in about 18 months.
When these famous car models debuted.Toyota Corolla: The best-selling car nameplate in history, with well over 50 million sold worldwide.
When these famous car models debuted.Range Rover: Its 1970 launch paired coil-spring off-road ability with comfort, and invented the idea of the luxury SUV.
When these famous car models debuted.DeLorean DMC-12: Its brushed stainless-steel body and gull-wing doors made it iconic, though its company collapsed within a couple of years.
When these famous car models debuted.Toyota Prius: The first mass-produced hybrid car, launched in Japan; its name is Latin for 'before'.
When these famous car models debuted.Tesla Model S: This all-electric sedan proved EVs could have long range and quick acceleration, and helped make Tesla a household name.

Rockets by height.Goddard's 1926 rocket: Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fueled rocket in Massachusetts, and it flew for just 2.5 seconds.
Rockets by height.German V-2: Germany's WWII missile was the first human-made object to reach space, in 1944.
Rockets by height.Rocket Lab Electron: Launched from New Zealand's Mahia Peninsula, this small-satellite workhorse has tried catching boosters with helicopters.
Rockets by height.Mercury-Redstone: It carried Alan Shepard on America's first crewed spaceflight in 1961, a 15-minute suborbital hop.
Rockets by height.Vostok rocket: It launched Yuri Gagarin in April 1961, the first human in space.
Rockets by height.Space Shuttle stack: An orbiter plus an orange tank and two boosters; the tank was the only large part thrown away.
Rockets by height.Falcon 9: Its first stage lands upright and is reflown, dramatically cutting launch costs.
Rockets by height.SLS (Block 1): NASA's Space Launch System sent Artemis I around the Moon uncrewed in November 2022.
Rockets by height.Soviet N1: The Soviet Moon rocket failed in all four test launches, costing the USSR the Moon race.
Rockets by height.Saturn V: It launched every Apollo Moon mission and stood taller than the Statue of Liberty.

Tennis by the numbers.Net height at centre (ft): The net sags to 3 ft in the middle, held down by a center strap, from 3.5 ft at the posts.
Tennis by the numbers.Grand Slams per year: The Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon and US Open make up the set; Steffi Graf won all four in 1988.
Tennis by the numbers.Points to win a tiebreak: Win by two points; the tiebreak was invented by James Van Alen in the 1960s.
Tennis by the numbers.Baseline to service line (ft): This is the zone known as 'no man's land', where many groundstrokes bounce and players are caught out.
Tennis by the numbers.Service line to net (ft): A serve must land in the box diagonally across the net, and these boxes extend 21 ft from it.
Tennis by the numbers.Singles court width (ft): Doubles adds side alleys of 4.5 ft on each side, called tramlines, to this width.
Tennis by the numbers.Doubles court width (ft): The Bryan brothers won 16 Grand Slam men's doubles titles together on the wider court.
Tennis by the numbers.Net height at posts (in): The posts stand a yard outside the doubles sidelines, and the Hawk-Eye cameras now judge line calls.
Tennis by the numbers.Court length (ft): The rectangle was standardized in the 1870s, replacing Major Wingfield's original hourglass shape.
Tennis by the numbers.Wimbledon singles draw: Seven rounds of knockout play find the champion, and Wimbledon, on grass, requires mostly white clothing.

How many is that?.A brace: A pair of creatures, most often ducks or pheasants. In old English hunting language a brace was a count of two game birds.
How many is that?.A hat-trick: In hockey and soccer, three goals by one player in a game. The term comes from cricket, where a bowler who took three wickets got a new hat.
How many is that?.A dozen: Eggs, months and inches in a foot all come in twelves. Some think base-12 counting began by tallying the finger segments of one hand with the thumb.
How many is that?.A baker's dozen: Bakers once added one extra loaf to avoid being penalized for short weight, which is why it is also called a long dozen.
How many is that?.A score: Abraham Lincoln's "four score and seven years ago" means 87. The word comes from an old practice of counting by notching sticks in twenties.
How many is that?.A gross: Twelve dozen. It was widely used in commerce for goods like pencils and buttons, and it comes from the French for "big" or "large".
How many is that?.A ream (of paper): Five hundred sheets, though a ream was once 480 or 500. A modern ream of office paper weighs about 2.5 kg for the common A4 size.
How many is that?.A great gross: Twelve gross, or 12 times 144. It was used for wholesale trade in things like buttons and pins.
How many is that?.A myriad: Greek for "ten thousand", and in Chinese the word for it, wan, also means "countless". In modern English it often just means a great many.
How many is that?.A googol: A one followed by a hundred zeros. A nine-year-old, Milton Sirotta, coined the name in the 1920s, and it inspired the name of Google.

Inventions by women, in order.Hand-crank ice cream maker: Nancy Johnson patented the hand-cranked freezer in 1843, which made ice cream far easier to make at home. She sold the rights for $200.
Inventions by women, in order.Flat-bottom paper bag machine: Margaret Knight invented the machine that folds flat-bottomed paper bags, and later won a patent fight with a man who copied her. She held over 20 patents.
Inventions by women, in order.Improved life raft: Maria Beasley improved the lifeboat and later patented a barrel-making machine, and she became a wealthy inventor.
Inventions by women, in order.Windscreen wiper: Mary Anderson invented the wiper after seeing a streetcar driver struggling with snow in New York, and was initially told it wasn't useful.
Inventions by women, in order.Chocolate chip cookie: Ruth Wakefield, of the Toll House Inn in Massachusetts, invented the cookie by adding chopped chocolate to dough, then sold the idea to Nestle.
Inventions by women, in order.Frequency hopping (Lamarr): The Hollywood star and composer George Antheil patented a radio method that hops between frequencies, an ancestor of ideas used in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
Inventions by women, in order.Waterproof diaper cover: Marion Donovan made a waterproof diaper cover from a shower curtain, and it led to her idea for the disposable diaper, which she sold in 1951.
Inventions by women, in order.Liquid Paper: Bette Nesmith Graham, a typist and mother of Michael Nesmith of the Monkees, created the typewriter correction fluid in her kitchen.
Inventions by women, in order.Kevlar: Stephanie Kwolek, a DuPont chemist, invented the lightweight fiber, which is five times stronger than steel by weight, and is used in bulletproof vests.
Inventions by women, in order.Home security system: Marie Van Brittan Brown invented a home system with cameras and a peephole, the forerunner of modern video security, and filed for it in 1966.

Energy packed into each kilogram.Lithium-ion battery: A lithium-ion battery stores far less energy per kilogram than fuel, which is why electric cars need such heavy battery packs.
Energy packed into each kilogram.TNT: TNT's reputation comes from releasing its energy in an instant, not from storing a lot; coal holds about five times more per kilogram.
Energy packed into each kilogram.Dry wood: Dry wood stores much less energy than coal, and it's what humans have burned for hundreds of thousands of years.
Energy packed into each kilogram.Coal: Coal fueled the Industrial Revolution and packs roughly twice the energy of the same weight of dry wood.
Energy packed into each kilogram.Ethanol: Made by fermenting crops such as corn and sugarcane, it carries about two-thirds of gasoline's energy per kilogram.
Energy packed into each kilogram.Body fat: Your body stores energy mostly as fat, which holds more than twice as much per gram as carbohydrate.
Energy packed into each kilogram.Gasoline: Gasoline contains lots of energy for its weight, which is why the car is such a convenient way to move heavy loads.
Energy packed into each kilogram.Methane: The main component of natural gas, burning it releases more energy per kilogram than gasoline does.
Energy packed into each kilogram.Hydrogen: The lightest element packs the most chemical energy per kilogram, but it takes up huge space unless compressed or chilled.
Energy packed into each kilogram.Uranium-235 (fission): Splitting a kilogram of this isotope releases millions of times more energy than burning fuel, which is how nuclear plants work.

Film franchises, by their first movie.Godzilla: Gojira was a metaphor for nuclear fears after Hiroshima, and the franchise is among the longest running.
Film franchises, by their first movie.Planet of the Apes: Its twist ending, with a ruined Statue of Liberty, is among film's most famous; it was based on a Pierre Boulle novel.
Film franchises, by their first movie.Rocky: Stallone wrote it himself and it won Best Picture; fans still run up the Philadelphia museum steps.
Film franchises, by their first movie.Mad Max: Made for about A$350,000, it launched Mel Gibson's career.
Film franchises, by their first movie.The Terminator: Cameron said the idea came from a feverish dream of a metal skeleton rising from fire.
Film franchises, by their first movie.Mission: Impossible: It adapted a 1960s TV series, and Tom Cruise does many of his own stunts.
Film franchises, by their first movie.Pirates of the Caribbean: It is based on the Disney theme park ride that opened in 1967.
Film franchises, by their first movie.Twilight: Author Stephenie Meyer says the idea came from a vivid dream.
Film franchises, by their first movie.The Hunger Games: Based on Suzanne Collins's novels, with Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss.
Film franchises, by their first movie.John Wick: Directed by former stuntmen Chad Stahelski and David Leitch.

Dynamic markings by loudness.Pianissississimo: The suffix '-issimo' means 'very', so each extra 'iss' stacks another level of quiet. Tchaikovsky once wrote a bassoon passage marked pppppp.
Dynamic markings by loudness.Pianississimo: It's rarely written, as the sound is barely above silence, so performers must nearly whisper through their instruments.
Dynamic markings by loudness.Pianissimo: The 'pp' sign gives the soft, hushed sound that makes a sudden loud chord land like a shock.
Dynamic markings by loudness.Piano: The instrument's full name is 'pianoforte', meaning 'soft-loud', because unlike the harpsichord it could vary its volume.
Dynamic markings by loudness.Mezzo-piano: 'Mezzo' means 'half' in Italian, as in mezzo-soprano, so this means moderately soft rather than very soft.
Dynamic markings by loudness.Mezzo-forte: It's relative rather than a fixed volume, and the real loudness depends on the instrument, room and piece.
Dynamic markings by loudness.Forte: Written dynamics only became common in the 1600s, and Gabrieli's 1597 Sonata pian e forte is an early example of such contrasts.
Dynamic markings by loudness.Fortissimo: At ff, a large orchestra can top 100 decibels, about as loud as a power tool.
Dynamic markings by loudness.Fortississimo: Mahler's symphonies, with their huge orchestras, use it for their biggest climaxes.
Dynamic markings by loudness.Fortissississimo: Extremely rare, it is basically an order to play as loudly as the instrument can safely manage.

Milestones in the AI business.Deep Blue beats Kasparov: IBM's chess computer beat the reigning world champion 3.5 to 2.5, in a 1997 rematch after Kasparov won the first match in 1996.
Milestones in the AI business.DeepMind founded: Demis Hassabis and two co-founders started it in London, and Google bought it in 2014.
Milestones in the AI business.Siri debuts: It began as an independent app before Apple bought it, and arrived as a built-in feature of the iPhone 4S.
Milestones in the AI business.Amazon Alexa debuts: It came with the Echo speaker, and its name was reportedly inspired by the Library of Alexandria.
Milestones in the AI business.OpenAI founded: It began as a non-profit research lab, with backers including Sam Altman and Elon Musk.
Milestones in the AI business.AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol: It won four games out of five against a Go legend, and its surprising 'Move 37' stunned human experts.
Milestones in the AI business.GPT-3 released: With 175 billion parameters it was far larger than its predecessors, and could write essays and code from short prompts.
Milestones in the AI business.Anthropic founded: Former OpenAI staff, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, started it, with an emphasis on AI safety.
Milestones in the AI business.ChatGPT launches: It reached a million users in about five days and an estimated 100 million within two months.
Milestones in the AI business.Google Gemini launches: Built by Google DeepMind and named for the twins constellation, it was designed to handle text, images and audio together.

When these famous bridges opened.Ponte Vecchio, Florence: The only bridge in Florence to survive the 1944 German retreat, it is lined with jewellers because butchers were banned from its shops in 1593.
When these famous bridges opened.Rialto Bridge, Venice: Venice's most famous bridge was built from stone after earlier wooden ones collapsed, and its design beat entries by Michelangelo and Palladio.
When these famous bridges opened.The Iron Bridge, Shropshire: The world's first major cast-iron bridge was raised over the Severn Gorge, and its success helped launch the Industrial Revolution era of iron building.
When these famous bridges opened.Brooklyn Bridge: It was the first steel-wire suspension bridge. Before opening, P. T. Barnum marched 21 elephants across it to prove it was safe.
When these famous bridges opened.Forth Bridge: This red cantilever bridge in Scotland needs constant repainting, which led to the saying 'painting the Forth Bridge' for any endless chore.
When these famous bridges opened.Tower Bridge: It looks medieval, but the Victorian steel skeleton hides behind stone cladding; the high walkways originally let pedestrians cross when the bascules were raised.
When these famous bridges opened.Sydney Harbour Bridge: Locals call it the Coathanger. Its steel arch is among the widest of its kind, and it opened a year before the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco.
When these famous bridges opened.Golden Gate Bridge: Its colour is officially 'International Orange', chosen partly because it stands out in the fog and goes well with the surrounding hills.
When these famous bridges opened.Øresund Bridge: It is a bridge and a tunnel in one, linking Denmark and Sweden, and it appeared in the Scandinavian crime drama The Bridge.
When these famous bridges opened.Millau Viaduct: At about 343 metres it is the tallest bridge in the world, higher than the Eiffel Tower, and it can rise above the clouds in southern France.

Alcohol content of these liqueurs and od.White Claw hard seltzer: The hard seltzer had a viral summer in 2019, when stores ran out and the beverage industry paid attention.
Alcohol content of these liqueurs and od.Aperol: The Italian aperitif is bright orange and bittersweet, and it is the main ingredient of the spritz.
Alcohol content of these liqueurs and od.Sake: Rice wine is brewed more like beer than wine, as starch is converted to sugar by mould, and it can be served hot or cold.
Alcohol content of these liqueurs and od.Midori: The bright green melon liqueur was a hit at 1980s parties, and it was launched in Las Vegas.
Alcohol content of these liqueurs and od.Disaronno: The almond-flavoured Italian liqueur has no almonds, as it is made from apricot kernels, and the bottle is square.
Alcohol content of these liqueurs and od.Jägermeister: The German herbal liqueur is made from 56 herbs and spices, and it is claimed that its stag logo is a hunting patron saint.
Alcohol content of these liqueurs and od.Fernet-Branca: The bitter Italian amaro is a favourite of bartenders, and in Argentina it is mixed with cola.
Alcohol content of these liqueurs and od.Green Chartreuse: Monks in France have made this herbal liqueur since 1764 from 130 plants, and the colour green was named after it.
Alcohol content of these liqueurs and od.Wray & Nephew Overproof: The Jamaican rum is a strong white spirit, and it is used in tiki drinks, and it is made in the Appleton region.
Alcohol content of these liqueurs and od.Spirytus Rektyfikowany: The Polish vodka is nearly pure alcohol, and it is mostly used for infusions, and it is banned in many places.

How long these journeys took.Luna 2 to the Moon: It was the first spacecraft to reach the Moon's surface, deliberately crashing there in 1959.
How long these journeys took.Apollo 11 to the Moon: Armstrong and Aldrin spent about 21 hours on the surface after this three-day trip.
How long these journeys took.Venus Express to Venus: ESA's first mission to Venus, it orbited the planet from 2006 until 2014.
How long these journeys took.Perseverance to Mars: It carried the Ingenuity helicopter and landed in Jezero crater in February 2021.
How long these journeys took.Hayabusa2 to Ryugu: The Japanese probe returned samples of this asteroid to Earth in 2020.
How long these journeys took.Juno to Jupiter: This solar-powered probe orbits Jupiter in a polar orbit, studying its clouds and magnetic field.
How long these journeys took.Cassini to Saturn: It dropped the Huygens probe onto Titan in 2005 and ended in 2017 by diving into Saturn.
How long these journeys took.New Horizons to Pluto: It sped past Pluto at about 14 km/s, revealing the dwarf planet's heart-shaped plain.
How long these journeys took.Voyager 2 to Neptune: The only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune, it flew past Neptune in 1989.
How long these journeys took.Voyager 1 to interstellar: It crossed into interstellar space in 2012, and it is the farthest human-made object.

When these places got their new names.New Amsterdam: The Dutch eventually kept Suriname in exchange for it, under the Treaty of Breda in 1667.
When these places got their new names.Edo: The seat of the Tokugawa shogunate, it was one of the world's largest cities by the 1700s, with about a million residents.
When these places got their new names.Persia: Reza Shah asked foreign governments to say Iran, a name that means land of the Aryans, instead of the Greek-derived Persia.
When these places got their new names.Siam: The new name Thailand means land of the free, and Siam was the name used on British maps and treaties.
When these places got their new names.Ceylon: It became Sri Lanka, meaning resplendent island, though Ceylon tea kept the old name on the label.
When these places got their new names.Saigon: In French colonial times it was nicknamed the Pearl of the Far East, and it was the capital of South Vietnam.
When these places got their new names.Burma: The military government changed it in 1989, and some countries and media still use the older name.
When these places got their new names.Leningrad: A vote restored the older name, and the Hermitage museum stands there in the former tsarist capital.
When these places got their new names.Bombay: The new name comes from a local goddess, and Bollywood is a playful blend of Bombay and Hollywood.
When these places got their new names.Swaziland: King Mswati III announced the change, meaning land of the Swazi, on the country's 50th year of independence.

Online marketplaces, by founding year.eBay: It started as AuctionWeb in 1995, and its first sale was reportedly a broken laser pointer for about 14 dollars.
Online marketplaces, by founding year.Alibaba: Jack Ma, a former English teacher, founded it in his Hangzhou apartment with a group of friends.
Online marketplaces, by founding year.Taobao: Alibaba launched it to take on eBay in China, and made it free for sellers.
Online marketplaces, by founding year.Etsy: Founded in Brooklyn, it is the home of handmade and vintage goods, with makers from all over the world.
Online marketplaces, by founding year.Shopify: It began as an online snowboard shop called Snowdevil before its founder built the shop software into a business.
Online marketplaces, by founding year.Vinted: This secondhand fashion marketplace was founded in Lithuania and now operates across Europe.
Online marketplaces, by founding year.Wish: Founded as ContextLogic, it became known for very cheap goods shipped from overseas.
Online marketplaces, by founding year.Depop: The fashion resale app began in Milan, was later based in London, and was bought by Etsy in 2021.
Online marketplaces, by founding year.StockX: It treats sneakers like stocks, showing live bid and ask prices, and was founded in Detroit.
Online marketplaces, by founding year.Temu: It was launched by the owner of Pinduoduo and became known for its Super Bowl ads and ultra-cheap goods.

Gothic and horror novels, by publication.The Castle of Otranto: Horace Walpole claimed it was a translation of a medieval Italian manuscript, and this kicked off the Gothic genre.
Gothic and horror novels, by publication.Frankenstein: Mary Shelley began it at 18 during a rainy summer at Lake Geneva, when friends challenged each other to write ghost stories.
Gothic and horror novels, by publication.The Fall of the House of Usher: Poe's short story features a house that cracks in two as its owner falls apart, with an unforgettable atmosphere.
Gothic and horror novels, by publication.Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde: Stevenson said the plot came to him in a dream, and the book sold tens of thousands of copies in six months.
Gothic and horror novels, by publication.The Picture of Dorian Gray: Wilde's only novel was quoted against him in his trials, as evidence of immorality.
Gothic and horror novels, by publication.Dracula: Bram Stoker took the name Dracula from a book on Wallachia, where Vlad the Impaler ruled.
Gothic and horror novels, by publication.The Turn of the Screw: Henry James left it ambiguous whether the ghosts are real or the governess is losing her mind.
Gothic and horror novels, by publication.Rebecca: Its first line, Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again, is among the best known, and Hitchcock's film won Best Picture.
Gothic and horror novels, by publication.The Haunting of Hill House: Shirley Jackson's story of a haunted mansion has an opening paragraph often cited as a model for horror.
Gothic and horror novels, by publication.The Exorcist: William Peter Blatty based it loosely on a reported 1949 case of possession, and the 1973 film terrified audiences.

When these prehistoric beasts were named.Megatherium: Cuvier named this giant ground sloth, the size of an elephant, from bones sent to Spain from Argentina.
When these prehistoric beasts were named.Pterodactylus: Cuvier named it, the first pterosaur ever identified, and it was a flying reptile, not a dinosaur.
When these prehistoric beasts were named.Plesiosaurus: Mary Anning found the first complete plesiosaur skeleton on the Dorset coast, at Lyme Regis, in 1823.
When these prehistoric beasts were named.Iguanodon: The second dinosaur ever named; early reconstructions put its thumb spike on its nose like a horn.
When these prehistoric beasts were named.Hadrosaurus: The first nearly complete dinosaur skeleton found in North America turned up in New Jersey, now the state dinosaur.
When these prehistoric beasts were named.Brontosaurus: Long thought to be a mistake for Apatosaurus, Brontosaurus was revived as a valid genus in a 2015 study.
When these prehistoric beasts were named.Brachiosaurus: Its front legs were longer than the hind legs, like a giraffe's, and it starred in Jurassic Park.
When these prehistoric beasts were named.Parasaurolophus: Its long, hollow crest may have worked like a trumpet, making low calls to others of its kind.
When these prehistoric beasts were named.Giganotosaurus: This Argentine giant may have rivaled T. rex in size, and the name means giant southern lizard.
When these prehistoric beasts were named.Dreadnoughtus: Named for the battleships called dreadnoughts, because it feared nothing, this Patagonian sauropod is among the most complete giants found.

Great scientific voyages, by when they s.Cook's Endeavour: Captain James Cook sailed to Tahiti to watch Venus cross the Sun, then charted New Zealand's coast and the eastern coast of Australia.
Great scientific voyages, by when they s.Humboldt in the Americas: The German naturalist explored Venezuela and the Andes, and he climbed Chimborazo, and he later wrote the Cosmos.
Great scientific voyages, by when they s.HMS Beagle with Darwin: Darwin was just 22 on this five-year trip, and he returned with finches and tortoises that shaped the theory of evolution.
Great scientific voyages, by when they s.Wallace in Malay Archipelago: Alfred Russel Wallace independently conceived natural selection while collecting specimens in this region, and he drew the Wallace Line.
Great scientific voyages, by when they s.HMS Challenger expedition: This British round-the-world cruise discovered thousands of new species, and the Mariana Trench's Challenger Deep is named after the ship.
Great scientific voyages, by when they s.Nansen's Fram drift: The Norwegian explorer deliberately let his ship freeze into Arctic ice, to drift across the polar sea.
Great scientific voyages, by when they s.Kon-Tiki raft: Thor Heyerdahl sailed a balsa raft from Peru toward Polynesia to show ancient voyages might have been possible.
Great scientific voyages, by when they s.Trieste in Mariana Trench: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh descended to the deepest point in the ocean in a bathyscaphe, nearly 11 km down.
Great scientific voyages, by when they s.Alvin dives to the Titanic: Robert Ballard's team used the submersible to explore the Titanic wreck, which was found the year before.
Great scientific voyages, by when they s.Cameron's Deepsea Challenger: The filmmaker made a solo dive to the Mariana Trench in a green submarine, reaching nearly 11 km.

When these warships were launched.Mary Rose: Henry VIII's flagship sank in 1545 in view of the king, and was raised in 1982 and now sits in a museum.
When these warships were launched.Vasa: Sweden's warship sank on its maiden voyage after sailing about 1,300 m, being top-heavy; it was recovered in 1961.
When these warships were launched.USS Constitution: 'Old Ironsides' still floats in Boston as the oldest commissioned warship afloat.
When these warships were launched.HMS Warrior: Britain's first ironclad battleship made wooden fleets obsolete and is now a museum in Portsmouth.
When these warships were launched.USS Monitor: Its revolving turret and flat deck fought the Confederate ironclad Virginia to a draw at Hampton Roads.
When these warships were launched.HMS Dreadnought: Its all-big-gun design made earlier battleships obsolete, and was built in about a year.
When these warships were launched.Yamato: The largest battleship ever built, with 18.1-inch guns, sunk in 1945 on a near one-way mission off Okinawa.
When these warships were launched.USS Missouri: Japan's surrender was signed on its deck in Tokyo Bay in 1945, and it is now a museum at Pearl Harbor.
When these warships were launched.USS Enterprise (CVN-65): The first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, the 'Big E' had eight reactors and served about 51 years.
When these warships were launched.USS Gerald R. Ford: Lead ship of a new class, with electromagnetic catapults instead of steam.

How tall these rockets stand.V-2: Germany's WWII V-2 was the first long-range ballistic missile, and a 1944 test flight made it the first human-made object to reach space.
How tall these rockets stand.Rocket Lab Electron: Rocket Lab's Electron launches mostly from New Zealand, and the company has tried snatching its descending boosters mid-air with a helicopter.
How tall these rockets stand.Mercury-Redstone: This rocket lifted Alan Shepard in 1961 on America's first crewed spaceflight, a suborbital hop of about 15 minutes.
How tall these rockets stand.Mercury-Atlas: An Atlas rocket like this carried John Glenn in 1962, making him the first American to orbit Earth, three times around.
How tall these rockets stand.Soyuz: The Soyuz family has flown since the 1960s and is among the most-launched rocket designs ever, still ferrying crews to the space station.
How tall these rockets stand.Space Shuttle stack: Only the orbiter and two boosters were reused; the huge orange external tank was dropped and burned up on every flight.
How tall these rockets stand.Falcon 9: Its first stage can land upright on a drone ship or pad and fly again, with some boosters reflown many times.
How tall these rockets stand.NASA SLS: NASA's Space Launch System first flew in 2022 on Artemis I, sending an uncrewed Orion capsule around the Moon and back.
How tall these rockets stand.Saturn V: Still the tallest rocket to have carried astronauts, it stood taller than the Statue of Liberty including its pedestal, and sent crews to the Moon.
How tall these rockets stand.SpaceX Starship (full stack): Starship, a fully reusable design, is the tallest and most powerful rocket ever flown, and its booster is caught by the launch tower's arms.

Japanese numbers, by the value they name.ni: Japanese has two number systems: native ones like futatsu, and Chinese-derived ones like ni, used for counting numbers and dates.
Japanese numbers, by the value they name.san: The same word, san, also works as a polite suffix after names, as in Tanaka-san, though it's written with different characters.
Japanese numbers, by the value they name.go: It also names the ancient board game Go, though that game's name is written with a different character.
Japanese numbers, by the value they name.roku: The Tokyo district Roppongi means "six trees", from the roku in its name.
Japanese numbers, by the value they name.nana: The Shichi-Go-San festival celebrates children aged three, five and seven, and seven can be said nana or shichi.
Japanese numbers, by the value they name.hachi: The character for eight widens toward the bottom, which is why the number is seen as lucky.
Japanese numbers, by the value they name.kyū: Nine is said kyū rather than ku, because ku sounds like the word for suffering.
Japanese numbers, by the value they name.jū: In sumo, the second-highest division is named jūryō, literally ten ryo, an old unit of pay.
Japanese numbers, by the value they name.hyaku: Hundred-yen shops, the Japanese dollar stores, are named for it, with prices actually starting from 100 yen.
Japanese numbers, by the value they name.sen: In Spirited Away, Chihiro's name is shortened to Sen, taking the character for thousand from the first part of her name.

Unfinished works, by when work on them s.The Canterbury Tales: Chaucer left his unfinished frame story of pilgrims on the way to Canterbury, and only 24 of a planned 120 or so tales were written.
Unfinished works, by when work on them s.Michelangelo's Rondanini Pietà: Michelangelo worked on it until days before he died, aged 88, and its unfinished figures seem to merge into one another.
Unfinished works, by when work on them s.Mozart's Requiem: Mozart died while writing the Requiem, and his student Süssmayr finished it, though exactly how much he wrote remains debated.
Unfinished works, by when work on them s.Austen's Sanditon: Jane Austen worked on this novel about a seaside resort until illness forced her to stop, and she died in July 1817.
Unfinished works, by when work on them s.Schubert's Unfinished Symphony: Schubert wrote only two movements of this symphony, and it was found in a drawer decades after his death.
Unfinished works, by when work on them s.The Mystery of Edwin Drood: Charles Dickens died partway through this murder mystery, leaving readers to debate who was responsible for the crime.
Unfinished works, by when work on them s.Kafka's The Castle: Kafka's unfinished novel is about a land surveyor who can never reach the castle that controls the village.
Unfinished works, by when work on them s.Puccini's Turandot: Puccini died of cancer before completing his final opera, and Franco Alfano finished it; at the premiere, conductor Toscanini stopped where Puccini had.
Unfinished works, by when work on them s.Fitzgerald's The Last Tycoon: Fitzgerald was writing this Hollywood novel when he died of a heart attack, and Edmund Wilson edited the manuscript for publication.
Unfinished works, by when work on them s.Wallace's The Pale King: David Foster Wallace left this novel about IRS workers unfinished at his death, and it was published with his notes.

Esperanto numbers, by the value they nam.du: L. L. Zamenhof published Esperanto in 1887, hoping to give people a neutral second language that belonged to nobody.
Esperanto numbers, by the value they nam.tri: Esperanto's numbers borrow from Latin and Romance languages, so 'tri' looks familiar to anyone who knows Spanish or French.
Esperanto numbers, by the value they nam.kvar: It is close to the Latin 'quattuor' and the French 'quatre', and every Esperanto number is a single short, regular word.
Esperanto numbers, by the value they nam.kvin: It resembles the Latin 'quinque' and the French 'cinq', and it is the root for words like 'kvina', meaning fifth.
Esperanto numbers, by the value they nam.ses: It is close to the Latin 'sex' and the French 'six', and the Esperanto number can be used as a prefix or suffix on its own.
Esperanto numbers, by the value they nam.sep: It matches Latin 'septem' and French 'sept', so a French or Spanish speaker can often guess it straight away.
Esperanto numbers, by the value they nam.ok: It is a short form of the Latin 'octo', which is also where 'octopus' and 'octagon' get their eight.
Esperanto numbers, by the value they nam.naŭ: The letter 'u with a breve', used here, is sounded like an English 'w', as in the 'ow' of 'cow'.
Esperanto numbers, by the value they nam.dek: Multiples are built by adding it on, so 'dudek' is twenty and 'tridek' thirty, a very regular system.
Esperanto numbers, by the value they nam.cent: It comes from the Latin centum, just like 'cent' and 'century', and Esperanto uses 'mil' for a thousand.

Bones of the human body by length.Stapes (stirrup): The smallest bone in the body sits in the middle ear and takes its name from its stirrup shape; it passes sound to the inner ear.
Bones of the human body by length.Malleus (hammer): Its name is Latin for hammer; it taps the incus, or anvil, in the chain of three tiny bones that carry sound.
Bones of the human body by length.Pinky fingertip bone: Each finger except the thumb has three bones; with 27 in each hand, your hands hold over a quarter of your skeleton.
Bones of the human body by length.Patella (kneecap): A sesamoid bone embedded in a tendon, it protects the knee and adds leverage; babies are born with only cartilage there.
Bones of the human body by length.Calcaneus (heel): The biggest bone of the foot takes the first impact of every step, and the Achilles tendon attaches to it.
Bones of the human body by length.Clavicle (collarbone): The only long bone lying sideways, it is among the most commonly broken bones, especially in children.
Bones of the human body by length.Ulna (forearm): It forms the point of your elbow; the funny-bone tingle comes from the ulnar nerve running nearby.
Bones of the human body by length.Humerus (upper arm): Its name comes from the Latin for shoulder, and merely sounds like humorous; the ball joint at its top gives the shoulder huge range.
Bones of the human body by length.Tibia (shin): The second-longest bone carries most of the lower leg's weight, with the slim fibula alongside it.
Bones of the human body by length.Femur (thigh): The longest and strongest bone in the body is about a quarter of your height and can bear several times your weight.

When these religious orders were founded.Benedictines (Monte Cassino): Benedict's Rule, with its motto 'ora et labora' (pray and work), shaped monastic life; the abbey was bombed in 1944.
When these religious orders were founded.Cluny Abbey: This Burgundian abbey became the heart of a vast network of monasteries, with the biggest church in Christendom for centuries.
When these religious orders were founded.Carthusians: Founded by Bruno of Cologne, this order lives in near-silence, and its monks make the liqueur Chartreuse.
When these religious orders were founded.Cistercians: The monks, in white habits, followed Bernard of Clairvaux's lead, and a reformed branch gave us Trappist beer.
When these religious orders were founded.Knights Templar: They guarded pilgrims, grew immensely rich, and were arrested on Friday 13 October 1307 on the order of Philip IV.
When these religious orders were founded.Teutonic Knights: Founded at Acre in the Holy Land, they later ruled Prussia and built the great fortress of Marienburg.
When these religious orders were founded.Franciscans: Francis of Assisi started it, and is credited with creating the first live nativity scene in 1223.
When these religious orders were founded.Dominicans: Dominic's friars are punningly nicknamed 'Domini canes', the 'hounds of the Lord'.
When these religious orders were founded.Augustinian Friars: The order was formed in 1256 by merging several hermit groups; Martin Luther started out as a friar of this order.
When these religious orders were founded.Bridgettines: Founded by Swedish mystic Birgitta, its houses had both nuns and monks under the leadership of an abbess.

Your cosmic address, smallest to largest.Earth: It's the densest of all the planets of our solar system, with a diameter of about 12,742 km.
Your cosmic address, smallest to largest.The Moon's orbit: The Moon is slowly drifting away from us at around 3.8 centimetres a year.
Your cosmic address, smallest to largest.Neptune's orbit: Sunlight takes over four hours to reach this far, and the planet was first found by mathematics before telescopes saw it.
Your cosmic address, smallest to largest.The Oort Cloud: Never directly seen, it's a theorised shell of icy bodies; Voyager 1 would need about 300 years to reach its inner edge.
Your cosmic address, smallest to largest.Local Interstellar Cloud: The Sun has been moving through this wispy gas cloud of hydrogen and helium for some time, and may leave it in several thousand years.
Your cosmic address, smallest to largest.The Milky Way: Our galaxy has hundreds of billions of stars, and the Sun lies about 26,000 light-years from its centre.
Your cosmic address, smallest to largest.The Local Group: Home to the Milky Way, Andromeda and Triangulum, and Andromeda is approaching us, to merge in a few billion years.
Your cosmic address, smallest to largest.Virgo Supercluster: Our Local Group sits at its edge, and astronomers now regard it as part of a larger structure.
Your cosmic address, smallest to largest.Laniakea Supercluster: Its name is Hawaiian for 'immense heaven', and it was mapped in 2014 by tracing the flows of galaxies.
Your cosmic address, smallest to largest.Observable universe: It is far larger than the universe's age of 13.8 billion years would suggest, because space has expanded.

How long these leaders held power.John F. Kennedy: Kennedy's term was cut short by assassination in 1963. He was the youngest person ever elected US president, at age 43.
How long these leaders held power.Vladimir Lenin: Lenin led Russia's Bolsheviks after the 1917 revolution. He was the first head of the Soviet state and died in 1924 after a series of strokes.
How long these leaders held power.Margaret Thatcher: Thatcher was Britain's first female prime minister, and her 11 years made her the longest-serving PM of the 20th century.
How long these leaders held power.Benito Mussolini: Mussolini coined the term fascism and styled himself Il Duce. He was ousted in 1943 and killed by partisans in 1945.
How long these leaders held power.Mao Zedong: Mao founded the People's Republic of China in 1949. His Little Red Book became one of the most printed books in history.
How long these leaders held power.Francisco Franco: Franco won the Spanish Civil War and ruled until his death in 1975. Spain then quickly turned toward democracy under King Juan Carlos.
How long these leaders held power.Muammar Gaddafi: Gaddafi seized power in a 1969 coup at age 27. He kept a famous Bedouin tent and a female bodyguard unit, and fell in 2011.
How long these leaders held power.Kim Il-sung: Kim Il-sung founded North Korea in 1948. He is still honored as Eternal President, a title the country kept after his death in 1994.
How long these leaders held power.Fidel Castro: Castro led Cuba's 1959 revolution and survived hundreds of reported assassination plots. He handed over power to his brother Raul in 2008.
How long these leaders held power.Emperor Hirohito: Hirohito's reign, called Showa, spanned the Depression, World War II, and Japan's postwar boom. His 1945 radio broadcast announced surrender.

Great die-offs in Earth's history.End-Ediacaran: The End-Ediacaran event wiped out many of Earth's earliest large, soft-bodied organisms, just before the Cambrian explosion of life.
Great die-offs in Earth's history.End-Ordovician: The End-Ordovician event is blamed on glaciation and falling seas, and it killed nearly 85 percent of marine species.
Great die-offs in Earth's history.Late Devonian: The Late Devonian extinction hit reef builders and armored fish hard, and may have lasted millions of years in waves.
Great die-offs in Earth's history.End-Permian (Great Dying): The Great Dying killed around 90 percent of species. Massive Siberian volcanism is the leading suspect behind it.
Great die-offs in Earth's history.End-Triassic: The End-Triassic event cleared the way for dinosaurs, which then dominated the planet for over 130 million years.
Great die-offs in Earth's history.Toarcian event: The Toarcian event was a marine crisis linked to volcanic activity, warming seas and oceans with little oxygen.
Great die-offs in Earth's history.End-Cretaceous: An asteroid hit near Chicxulub in Mexico, ending the non-bird dinosaurs, and about three quarters of species died.
Great die-offs in Earth's history.Paleocene–Eocene heat spike: The PETM was a sudden global warming spike driven by a massive carbon release, yet it didn't cause a mass extinction of land life.
Great die-offs in Earth's history.Eocene–Oligocene cooling: This cooling coincided with Antarctica's ice sheets forming, and Europe's mammal fauna turned over in what's called the Grande Coupure.
Great die-offs in Earth's history.Ice Age megafauna vanish: Mammoths, giant sloths and saber-toothed cats disappeared as humans spread and the climate changed, and scientists still debate which mattered more.

When these famous restaurants first open.St. Peter Stiftskeller: A Salzburg restaurant claims a first written mention in 803. Mozart is said to have dined there.
When these famous restaurants first open.Honke Owariya, Kyoto: A Kyoto soba shop said to be over 550 years old, and it has served imperial households.

US kitchen measures.Smidgen: The smallest of the traditional pinch measures, about half a pinch. Some cooks treat it as a lighter touch than a dash, and old recipes rarely agree.
US kitchen measures.Pinch: Roughly what you can grip between thumb and forefinger. Some measuring spoon sets include a pinch spoon, but cooks usually just do it by eye.
US kitchen measures.Dash: A bit more than a pinch, or a quick shake from a bottle. Bartenders use it for bitters, and the exact size still depends on the bottle and the hand.
US kitchen measures.Teaspoon: A cooking teaspoon is a measure, not the spoon in your cutlery drawer, which varies widely. Three of them make one tablespoon.
US kitchen measures.Tablespoon: Three teaspoons to a tablespoon, and sixteen tablespoons to a cup. Australia uses a larger one of 20 ml, so imported recipes can taste off.
US kitchen measures.Fluid ounce: The word fluid matters, since it measures volume, not weight. The US fluid ounce is slightly larger than the British imperial one.
US kitchen measures.Cup: The US cup is about 237 ml, but a metric cup elsewhere is 250 ml. That small gap is enough to change a cake if you're not careful.
US kitchen measures.Pint: Two cups make a pint, but a US pint is smaller than a British one. The British imperial pint is about 568 ml, so a pub pint differs from an American one.
US kitchen measures.Quart: The name comes from the Latin for a fourth, since it is a quarter of a gallon. Two pints make one quart.
US kitchen measures.Gallon: The US gallon is about 3.79 litres, while the British imperial gallon is about 4.55. Four quarts fill it, and it's a unit that exists almost only in America now.
